front.title: DCARP: Distributing Dynamic Addresses to CARP Redundancy Groups

abstract.t: The Common Address Redundancy Protocol (CARP) lets a group of hosts share IP addresses, but every member must be configured with the shared addresses in advance. When the shared address is assigned dynamically, for example by DHCP to the current master, the backups do not know it, and since CARP authenticates its advertisements over the shared addresses, a change of the address splits the group into several masters. The Distributed Common Address Redundancy Protocol (DCARP) lets the master distribute the shared IPv4 address, its netmask and the gateway of its network, together with the master's address on another network the members share, which they route through while they are backups, to the other members, encrypted and authenticated, and resolves the split that follows an address change.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: CARP , like VRRP , makes a group of hosts share one or more virtual addresses on a network. One member, the Master, owns the addresses and answers for them; the others, the Backups, take over when the Master stops sending advertisements. CARP requires that all members are configured with the same virtual addresses.

That requirement cannot be met when the shared address is assigned dynamically. A typical case is a pair of firewalls whose external address is assigned by an Internet service provider with DHCP : the DHCP client runs on the CARP interface of the Master, which shares a virtual MAC address with the Backups, and only the Master learns the address. Two problems follow:

ol.li: A Backup that becomes Master does not know the address, its netmask or the gateway of that network, and cannot use them until it completes a DHCP exchange of its own.

CARP authenticates its advertisements over the set of virtual addresses. When the Master's address changes, the Backups reject its advertisements, conclude that the Master is gone, and become Masters themselves. The group stays split until an operator intervenes.

section.t: A Backup cannot use the provider's gateway either: its CARP interface passes no traffic. It routes through the Master over another network the members share, typically an internal one, and needs the Master's address there.

DCARP solves these problems. The Master sends the address, its netmask, the gateway of its network and its own address on the shared network to the group, encrypted and authenticated with a shared key; every member applies the newest configuration it receives, whatever its CARP state. DCARP does not replace CARP: CARP still elects the Master, and DCARP only distributes what CARP needs to be configured with, and what the members need to route in either state.
This version of DCARP handles IPv4 only.

section.name: Requirements Language
section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

dl.dd: The interface of a member that carries the virtual address managed by DCARP.
The CARP states of a member's CARP interface. A CARP interface without any address does not take part in the election and stays in Init.
The virtual address, its netmask, the gateway on its network and a Backup Gateway, together with a Generation.
The address of the Master on another network that the members share, through which the other members route while they are Backups.
The time at which the address of a Configuration was obtained, used to decide which Configuration is the newest ().
The CARP demote count, advertisement base and advertisement skew of a member, which CARP uses to elect the Master. Lower values are better.
The interface on which a member sends and receives DCARP messages: the CARP interface unless configured otherwise ().

section.name: Protocol Overview
section.t: All members of a CARP group run DCARP and share a 256-bit key. The Master sends a DCARP message to an IPv4 multicast group on the Sync interface when it becomes Master, when the address of its CARP interface changes, and periodically. The message carries the Master's Configuration, its Priority, and fields that let receivers detect replays. It is encrypted and authenticated with XChaCha20-Poly1305.

A member that receives a valid message takes the Configuration if its Generation is newer than its own, in every CARP state, so a Backup that has become Master because it rejected the Master's advertisements still takes the new address. Of the same Generation, a member that is not Master takes it from any sender, since CARP has elected the sender; a Master takes it only if the sender has a better Priority, or if its CARP interface has no IPv4 address. Taking a Configuration makes its address the only IPv4 address of the CARP interface, which restarts CARP on that interface; with the same addresses as the Master, the member then accepts the Master's advertisements and returns to Backup.
DCARP does not change routes. It makes the Configuration available to the local system, which uses the gateway when the member becomes Master ().

section.name: Wire Format
section.t: A DCARP message is the payload of a UDP datagram and is exactly 104 octets long:
The Ciphertext and Authentication Tag are the output of AEAD_XChaCha20_Poly1305 over the 64-octet plaintext of , as described in .

section.name: Plaintext
section.t: All integers are unsigned and in network byte order unless stated otherwise.

dl.dd: 1, Configuration. No other type is defined.
The IPv4 address of the sender's CARP interface.
Its netmask.
The IPv4 address of the gateway on the network of the Address that a member is to use as Master, or 0.0.0.0 if the sender knows none ().
The sender's IPv4 address on another network that the members share, which the other members are to use as gateway while they are Backups, or 0.0.0.0 if there is none.

The number of seconds the DHCP lease of the Address lasts from the Generation on, or 0 if the sender knows of no lease. Receivers MAY use it, for example to tell when the lease runs out. The field was reserved before, so that earlier senders set it to zero and earlier receivers ignore it.
A random value the sender chooses when it starts, which identifies it for replay detection.
A counter of the sender, 1 in its first message and incremented by one in each message it sends.
The time the message was sent, as a signed number of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z.
The Generation of the Configuration, a signed number of seconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z, or 0 ().
dl.dt: Demote (4 octets), Advbase (1 octet), Advskew (1 octet):
dl.dd: The sender's CARP demote count, advertisement base and advertisement skew: its Priority.
Senders MUST set it to zero; receivers MUST ignore it.

section.name: Encryption and Authentication
section.t: All members of a group share a 256-bit key. How the key is generated and distributed is outside the scope of this document; it MUST have at least 256 bits of entropy .
A sender encrypts and authenticates each plaintext with AEAD_XChaCha20_Poly1305 , which extends the AEAD construction of to a 192-bit nonce. The inputs are:

dl.dd: The shared key.
24 octets the sender MUST choose at random for each message. With 192 bits, random nonces do not repeat in practice, and no state is needed to keep them unique.
The 8 octets of the ASCII string "DCARP 1" followed by a zero octet, which binds the key to this protocol and version.
The 64 octets of .

section.t: The message is the nonce, followed by the ciphertext and the 16-octet authentication tag. A receiver MUST authenticate a message before it uses any of its contents, and MUST discard messages that fail.

section.name: Transport
section.t: Messages are sent as UDP datagrams to the IPv4 multicast group 224.0.0.18, destination port 3522, with a time to live of 1 ( discusses these values). An implementation SHOULD allow both to be configured.

By default the Sync interface is the CARP interface. An implementation MAY allow another interface to be configured, for example a dedicated link between the members. A member MUST join the group on its Sync interface, and MUST select the interface explicitly rather than by address: the address of the CARP interface changes, and may be missing. It MUST discard messages received on any other interface, and messages whose payload is not exactly 104 octets.
A Master whose CARP interface is the Sync interface cannot send while CARP restarts after an address change (); it sends once it is Master again.

section.name: Generations
section.t: Every Configuration has a Generation: the time its address was obtained or its DHCP lease last renewed. Comparing Generations tells which of two Configurations is newer. A member keeps the Generation of the Configuration it holds:

ul.li: When it starts, the Generation is that of the Configuration it held before for the address its CARP interface has, which it keeps in stable storage, or 0 if there is none.

When the address of its CARP interface changes other than by DCARP, for example when the DHCP client obtains a new address, the Generation becomes the current time, or one more than the Generation it held if that is not earlier.
When it takes a Configuration (), it adopts the Configuration's Generation.

As Master, before sending, it learns from its DHCP client when the client last obtained or renewed the lease of the address. Each such time is a new Generation: that time, or one more than the Generation it held if that is not earlier. A renewal does not change the address, but is a new Generation, so that the other members learn of it.

section.t: While a member runs, its Generation never decreases. A member MUST NOT take the time at which a lease was stored, for example the modification time of a lease file, for the time of its latest renewal: DHCP clients commonly store a lease when they obtain it, but not when they renew it, so that a Backup's stored lease can be newer than the Master's Generation.
Generations use wall-clock time, so the members' clocks MUST be synchronized, for example with NTP; see also .

section.name: Sending
section.t: A member whose CARP interface is Master and has an IPv4 address sends a message with its Configuration:
The periodic messages let members that start later, or that missed a message, learn the Configuration. The Interval MUST be shorter than the maximum age of ; the RECOMMENDED value is 10 seconds.

The Address and Netmask are those of the CARP interface; if it has several IPv4 addresses, the sender uses one of them consistently. The Gateway is the one the provider of the address gives: the gateway of the member's default route if that route goes through the CARP interface, as a DHCP client adds from the lease. A member that has become Master may still route via the previous Master, through another interface; it then sends the Gateway of the Configuration it last took or sent, if that is on the network of the Address, and otherwise 0.0.0.0. The Gateway is not configured by the operator. The Backup Gateway is the sender's own address on another network the members share, which the operator configures, or 0.0.0.0. Demote, Advbase and Advskew are the sender's current CARP values; the demote count is the sum over the groups the CARP interface belongs to, as CARP computes it.

section.name: Validation
section.t: A member discards a message, and SHOULD log its source address and the reason at a limited rate, if:

ol.li: its Timestamp differs from the member's clock by more than the maximum age, 30 seconds; or

its Sequence is not higher than the highest Sequence accepted from the same Sender. A member MUST remember the Sequence of the Senders it heard from most recently, at least as many as the group has members and at least eight; a restarted member is a new Sender.

section.t: A copy of a message that the system delivers again through another CARP interface on the link of the Sync interface, as some CARP implementations do with multicast, is no error: the member discards it without logging.
A member ignores its own messages, whose Sender is its own, and discards messages of an unknown Message Type.

section.name: Acceptance
section.t: A member takes the Configuration of a valid message if:

ul.li: its Generation is greater than the member's Generation, in any CARP state, Master, Backup or Init;

its Generation equals the member's Generation and the member is Backup or Init. Only a Master sends, and CARP has elected it, possibly with a worse Priority than the member's, as when a member returns without preemption. A member in Init sends nothing, and one whose CARP interface has no address yet gets it this way (); or

its Generation equals the member's Generation, the member is Master, and the sender's Priority is better than the member's own: a lower Demote, or an equal Demote and a lower Advbase, or equal values of both and a lower Advskew, which is the order in which CARP compares advertisements; or an equal Priority and a lower Sender, compared as unsigned 64-bit integers; or whatever the Priority, if the member's CARP interface has no IPv4 address: CARP authenticates its advertisements over the addresses.

section.t: It MUST discard, and SHOULD log, any other. The Generation comes first because after a failover the member with the worse Priority may hold the newer lease; the Priority decides only between Configurations of the same Generation, and there only for members that are Master at the same time and receive each other's messages but not each other's advertisements, for example over a separate Sync interface while the network of the CARP interface is split: exactly one of them takes the other's Configuration.

section.name: Taking a Configuration
section.t: To take a Configuration, a member adopts its Generation and makes its Address, with its Netmask, the only IPv4 address of the CARP interface: it adds the address if it is missing and then removes all other IPv4 addresses of the interface. It MUST NOT keep an old address, since CARP authenticates over all addresses (), and it SHOULD add the new address before removing the old ones, since a CARP interface without an address leaves the election.

A member that is Backup SHOULD put the address of the Configuration it holds back when its CARP interface has no IPv4 address: shortly after something else removed it, such as its DHCP client at the expiry of a lease that it obtained while the member was Master, unless another address has turned up meanwhile; and when the interface becomes Backup without it. Without the address, CARP rejects the Master's advertisements: an interface that keeps another address, such as an IPv6 link-local one, makes the member Master beside the Master, and one without any leaves the election. A Master MUST NOT do so, since its address follows its DHCP lease.

Each change of the addresses restarts CARP on the interface, so a member MUST NOT change them when the address is already the only one, and SHOULD do nothing when the Configuration equals the one it took last. Periodic messages thus cause no changes.
A member MUST NOT change its routes because of a Configuration. It makes the Configuration available locally, including the sender's Backup Gateway ().

section.name: Interaction with CARP
section.t: CARP computes the authentication of its advertisements over, among other things, the sorted set of IPv4 addresses of the CARP interface . When the Master's address changes:

ol.li: CARP on the Master restarts: the interface passes through Init and Backup and becomes Master again after about three advertisement intervals. Meanwhile it neither sends advertisements nor, on the CARP interface, DCARP messages.

The Backups reject the Master's advertisements, whose authentication now covers a different set of addresses. A Backup whose master-down timer expires before it has the new address becomes Master as well.

When the Master is Master again, it sends its Configuration, whose Generation is newer. Every other member takes it, in its current state, and changes its address, which restarts CARP on its interface. With the same addresses as the Master it accepts the Master's advertisements and becomes Backup again.
A member that became Master in step 2 sends its own, older Configuration. The Master, and any member that already holds the new Configuration, discards it as older.

section.t: If the new Configuration reaches a Backup before its master-down timer expires, the Backup takes it as Backup and step 2 does not occur. If the message is lost, the periodic messages repeat it. The interruption of the Master's own service while CARP restarts is not avoided by DCARP.
A member whose CARP interface has no address stays in Init. Since a member takes Configurations in Init as well, such a member obtains its address from the Master and then joins the election.

section.name: Local Use of the Configuration
section.t: DCARP does not set routes, so that it does not compete with the tools that already follow CARP state changes on a member, such as a daemon that changes the default route when the CARP interface becomes Master or Backup. A member SHOULD make the Configuration it holds, as Master or Backup, available to such tools, for example in a file. When the member becomes Master, they can then route via the Gateway at once, before any DHCP exchange of the new Master completes; when it becomes Backup, via the Backup Gateway. describes how the reference implementation does this.

The Backup Gateway a member makes available is that of the member it last took a Configuration from, also while it is Master itself, and across restarts; its own is of no use to it. When it falls back to Backup, the tools route at once, before a message from the new Master arrives, and the members' addresses on the shared network do not change. A member that has never taken a Configuration has no Backup Gateway, and the tools need another default.

With more than two members, the Master can change while a member stays Backup: its own CARP state does not change, but its Backup Gateway does. Tools that act only on the member's CARP state changes miss this. A member SHOULD therefore notify the tools whenever the Configuration it holds changes, as well as when its CARP state changes.

ul.li: All members MUST use the same key, group and port, and Sync interfaces on the same network. Implementations SHOULD log a fingerprint of the key, such as the first octets of a hash of it, so that operators can compare the keys without revealing them.
The members' clocks MUST agree within the maximum age of 30 seconds, and closely enough that Generations compare correctly.

The DHCP client of the shared address runs on the CARP interface and gets no lease on Backups, whose CARP interface does not pass traffic. A DHCP client left running on a Backup removes the address when the lease it obtained as Master expires (). On some systems the DHCP client also changes the local resolver configuration; operators may want to prevent that on the CARP interface.

A member restarted without the Configuration it held has Generation 0. Until its address changes or it learns of its DHCP lease, the other members discard the Configuration it sends as Master if they hold a newer one.

section.name: Security Considerations
section.t: The shared key protects the confidentiality, integrity and authenticity of the Configurations. Every holder of the key is trusted: a holder can make the other members take any address and gateway by sending a Configuration with a later Generation, and the Backups by sending one with the same Generation. The compromise of one member therefore compromises the group, and the key needs the same protection as the members' administrative credentials.

The Timestamp and Sequence stop replays. A member discards a message older than 30 seconds, and a message whose Sequence it has already seen from the same Sender. Within 30 seconds, a recorded message can be replayed to a member that does not remember its Sender, for example after a restart; such a message carries a Configuration that was current 30 seconds earlier, and is discarded anyway if the member holds a newer Generation.

DCARP depends on synchronized clocks. An attacker who can move a member's clock, for example by attacking its time synchronization, can make it discard valid messages, accept older ones, or give its own Configurations Generations that win over newer ones.

The encryption hides the Configuration, the Sender, Sequence and Priority, but not the existence, size and timing of the messages or the source address of the sender, which is visible to anyone on the network of the Sync interface. With the default Sync interface that is the network of the shared address, often a provider's network. A separate Sync interface on a trusted network hides even that.

Anyone on that network can send datagrams to the group. Each costs the receiver one authentication attempt; implementations SHOULD limit the rate at which they log discarded messages. The time to live of 1 and the link-local multicast group keep the messages on the local network.
Nonces are random and 192 bits long, so their reuse under one key is negligibly likely.
Tools that set routes from a Configuration act on data that is authenticated, but chosen by another member.

section.name: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document makes no requests of IANA. The reference implementation uses the multicast group 224.0.0.18, which is assigned to VRRP and also used by CARP, and UDP port 3522, which is not registered for DCARP. A version of this document intended for wider deployment would need a port assignment from the Service Name and Transport Protocol Port Number Registry , and either a multicast group assignment or a justification for sharing the VRRP group.

section.name: Reference Implementation
section.t: dcarpd(8) implements DCARP on OpenBSD. It derives the 256-bit key as the SHA-256 hash of a key file, sends every 10 seconds, and remembers 64 Senders. As Master it asks dhcpleased(8) over its control socket, read-only as "dhcpleasectl -l" does, when the lease of the address was last acknowledged and how long it lasts; after a malformed answer or none, it does not ask again until it is told to, lest a dhcpleased whose messages differ take the question for a request for a new lease.
It writes the Configuration it holds to a state file of shell variable assignments, which it replaces atomically:
section.sourcecode: DCARP_INTERFACE=carp0 DCARP_ADDRESS=192.0.2.10 DCARP_NETMASK=255.255.255.0 DCARP_GATEWAY=192.0.2.1 DCARP_BACKUP_GATEWAY=192.168.1.2 DCARP_GENERATION=1793625676 DCARP_LEASE_TIME=86400 DCARP_LEASE_EXPIRES=1793712076
section.t: It starts with the Generation of the state file, and as Backup puts the address back as describes.

ifstated(8) sources the file and routes via DCARP_GATEWAY when the CARP interface becomes Master, and via DCARP_BACKUP_GATEWAY when it becomes Backup, so that its configuration is the same on every member. A complete ifstated configuration is distributed with the implementation. The Backup Gateway is the -g option of dcarpd.

With more than two members, dcarpd runs the program given with its -x option, with the state file and the CARP state as arguments, whenever it writes the state file and whenever the CARP state changes, one run at a time; the program sets the routes.

The implementation comes with regression tests that run two or three members in separate routing domains of one host, including the split of , failovers among three members, a member returning without preemption, Masters of equal Priority, replays, tampered and stale messages, messages with another key, a Backup that loses its address, and renewals of the lease.
